---
title: "Landslide mitigation: slope stability, avoided deaths, and their value"
format: html
---

## Purpose

Value the deaths that forest root cohesion averts by holding hillslopes together. The service is
computed as a difference between two runs of the same model on the same grid: one in which forest
roots reinforce the soil as the land-cover map says they do, and one in which root cohesion is
removed entirely. Everything else -- terrain, soil, rainfall, population, roads, and the fitted
statistical models -- is identical between the two, so the difference in predicted deaths is
attributable to root reinforcement alone.

This note describes what the code in `global_invest/landslide_mitigation/` does. The science is a
fold of `m-braaksma/landslide_mitigation` v0.2.0 (folded 2026-08-16); the arithmetic lives in
`landslide_mitigation_chain.py` as pure functions, the raster drivers in
`landslide_mitigation_functions.py`, and the pipeline in `landslide_mitigation_tasks.py`.

## Grid and inputs

Everything is computed on the **NSIDC EASE-Grid 2.0 global 1km grid** (EPSG:6933), built from the
authoritative `EASE2_M01km.gpd` grid definition rather than assumed. EASE-Grid is equal-area, so a
pixel count converts to real area by one constant multiply and no latitude weighting is needed
anywhere in the chain. Every input is warped onto that exact grid and then checked against it for
matching size, pixel resolution and projection before the model runs.

| Input | Source | Resampling onto the 1km grid |
|---|---|---|
| Elevation | SEALS `alt_m.tif` (shared base data) | average |
| Agro-ecological zones | FAO GAEZ v5 AEZ57 | mode (categorical) |
| Forest cover | ESA-CCI annual land cover | class weights, then average |
| Landslide events | UGLC point records | coordinate transform, not a warp |
| Population | LandScan, per year | sum (conserves counts) |
| Soil texture, organic carbon, bulk density | SoilGrids 0-5, 5-15, 15-30cm | thickness-weighted mean, then average |
| Saturated conductivity | HiHydroSoil 0-5, 5-15, 15-30cm | thickness-weighted mean, then average |
| Soil and sediment thickness | Pelletier/ORNL DAAC | average |
| Mean annual precipitation | WorldClim BIO12 (1970-2000 normal) | average |
| Annual maximum daily rainfall | ERA5-Land, per year | bilinear (upsampling) |
| Road density | GRIP4 total density, m/km² | bilinear (upsampling) |

The three soil-depth intervals are combined by their own thickness (5, 10 and 15cm), and only where
each interval has data, so a pixel missing the deepest layer is the mean of the two shallower ones
rather than a hole.

Forest cover enters as a **root-reinforcement weight**, not as a binary forest mask. Closed-canopy
and flooded tree-cover classes take weight 1; the two mosaic tree/shrub-herbaceous classes are 50/50
land cover and take 0.5; sparse tree cover below 15% takes 0, as being below meaningful root
reinforcement. Every other class is 0. Averaging that 0-1 weight field onto the 1km grid gives each
pixel a fractional forest share.

## Slope

Slope is computed with `gdal.DEMProcessing` (Horn 1981) from the **raw** elevation at four times the
target resolution (~250m) and then averaged down to 1km. Computing slope at 1km directly would
flatten exactly the terrain the model is about. Because the grid is already in metres, no
degree-to-metre scale factor enters.

The elevation used for the hydrology is separately pit-filled at 1km: the trusted 300m DEM is already
pit-filled, but averaging it down to 1km can create new local minima. D8 flow direction and flow
accumulation run on the pit-filled version, and the accumulated pixel count is scaled to an upslope
contributing area in m².

## Slope stability with and without forest roots

The stability model is the **infinite-slope** form used across the SHALSTAB / SINMAP / TRIGRS family.
For every pixel,

$$
SI \;=\; \frac{\tan\phi}{\tan\beta}
\;+\; \frac{c_{\text{soil}} + c_{\text{root}}}{\gamma\,h\,\sin\beta\,\cos\beta}
\;-\; \min\!\left(\frac{q}{T\,\sin\beta},\,1\right)
$$

where $\phi$ is the internal friction angle, $\beta$ the slope, $c_{\text{soil}}$ the soil's own
cohesion, $c_{\text{root}}$ the root reinforcement, $\gamma$ the soil unit weight, $h$ the soil
depth, $q$ the specific discharge and $T$ the transmissivity. The first term is friction against
geometry, the second is cohesion holding the slope together, and the third is the destabilising
effect of water. Higher $SI$ is more stable.

The four soil terms are derived from the mapped soil properties:

- **Friction angle** $\phi = 25 + (\text{sand}\% - \text{clay}\%)/20$, clipped to 15-40 degrees:
  sandier soils resist shear at a steeper angle than clay-rich ones.
- **Soil cohesion** $c_{\text{soil}} = 2 + 0.03\,\text{clay}\% + 0.1\,\text{organic carbon}\%$ kPa,
  clipped to 0-50 kPa.
- **Unit weight** $\gamma = \rho\,g$, converting SoilGrids bulk density in Mg/m³ to kN/m³.
- **Transmissivity** $T = K_{\text{sat}} \times h$, with HiHydroSoil's integer conductivity unscaled
  and converted to m/day first.

The specific discharge is static rather than event-based: the WorldClim annual rainfall total is
spread evenly over the year, applied to the pixel's upslope contributing area, and divided by the
cell width it enters through. The hydrological term is physically a saturation ratio, so it is capped
at 1; uncapped, the heavily right-skewed upslope area drives most pixels onto the stability floor.

**Root cohesion is the only thing that differs between the two runs.** It is
$c_{\text{root}} = \text{forest share} \times c_{\text{root,max}}$ with
$c_{\text{root,max}} = 5$ kPa in the `observed` run and $0$ in the `full_impacts` counterfactual.

Three exclusions and clips are part of the method rather than defensive coding, and each changes
results:

- Pixels flatter than **2 degrees** are excluded entirely. Infinite-slope theory does not apply
  there, and without the exclusion both the friction and hydrological terms blow up near
  $\beta = 0$ and swamp the forest-cover signal -- the median observed-versus-counterfactual
  difference was exactly zero before it was added.
- Slope is clipped to 0.5-89.5 degrees and the friction angle to 15-40 degrees before the
  trigonometry, since $\tan\beta$ goes to zero at flat and diverges near vertical.
- $SI$ itself is clipped to $[-10, 10]$.

The `observed` index is computed for every modelling year and the prediction year; the counterfactual
only for the prediction year, since a counterfactual has no meaning during calibration.

## Calibrating stability to landslide probability

Recorded landslides are rare relative to land pixels, so the hazard model is fitted on a **stratified
case-control sample** rather than on the whole grid.

Cases are UGLC events. The events are filtered to those with a usable location accuracy -- the
recorded accuracy must be present, positive, not one of the fill codes UGLC uses, and no coarser than
**1000m** -- and then reprojected to EASE-Grid metres. Several events can fall in one 1km pixel, so
within a year they are collapsed to one row per pixel carrying the highest fatality count of the
group: the model is fitted on pixel-years.

Controls are pixel-years drawn uniformly at random over the grid and kept only where the GAEZ raster
says there is land, at **25 controls per case**, with a fixed seed so the draw is reproducible. Each
row, case or control, is then sampled for its stability index, annual maximum daily rainfall,
population, slope, road density and GAEZ zone. Rows missing stability, rainfall or zone are dropped
-- most of them are the near-flat pixels the stability model excluded.

An ordinary logit of case status on stability index and extreme rainfall is fitted on the modelling
years. Its **slope coefficients are consistent** estimates of the population slopes, but its
intercept carries the oversampling of cases, so it is corrected (Prentice and Pyke 1979):

$$
\alpha_{\text{corrected}} \;=\; \alpha_{\text{raw}} \;-\; \log\!\frac{\tau/(1-\tau)}{\pi/(1-\pi)}
$$

$\tau$ is the case fraction in the sample. $\pi$ is the prevalence in the population, and it is not
assumed: it is counted from the UGLC annual panels themselves, as event pixel-years over
**SI-eligible** land pixel-years across the same years used for training. Restricting the denominator
to the pixels the stability model actually scores keeps the prevalence on the same population the
model predicts over. The per-year counts behind it are exported as an audit table.

To build those panels, each UGLC event is stamped onto the grid as a disc of its own location
accuracy rather than as a single pixel: the binary panel marks every pixel the disc covers, and the
mortality panel spreads the event's fatalities over the disc with a linear distance decay
$1 - d/r$, summed across events.

The fit is scored by AUC on the training years and on the held-out prediction year.

## Fatalities given a landslide

Severity is a **two-part hurdle model**, fitted only on realized landslides (the cases) in the
modelling years, on the same four covariates in both parts: log(1+population), extreme rainfall,
slope and road density.

- **Part A**, a logit, gives $\Pr(\text{fatalities} > 0 \mid \text{landslide})$. If the maximum
  likelihood fit fails on separation, it falls back to an L2-regularized fit; the coefficients are
  then shrunk toward zero and the standard errors are not comparable to an unpenalized fit, so that
  fallback is a point estimate rather than inference.
- **Part B**, an OLS on the fatal subsample, gives $E[\log(\text{fatalities}) \mid \text{fatal}]$.

Back-transforming part B needs care: $\exp$ of a predicted log understates the expectation by
Jensen's inequality. The correction is **Duan's (1983) smearing factor**, the mean of $\exp$ of the
part-B residuals, which estimates the bias from the residuals themselves rather than assuming
log-normal errors. Expected fatalities given a landslide are therefore

$$
E[\text{deaths} \mid \text{landslide}] \;=\;
\Pr(\text{fatal}) \times \exp\!\big(X\beta_B\big) \times \text{smearing}.
$$

A separate diagnostic refits both parts with the stability index in place of slope, to check whether
stability subsumes slope's information in severity. It is written to its own output and never
overwrites the production coefficients.

## Prediction and avoided mortality

Prediction runs tile by tile over the land-containing tiles of the grid (2000 pixels per side by
default), so the global rasters are assembled from independent pieces.

For each scenario, expected deaths per pixel-year are

$$
\text{deaths} \;=\; \Pr(\text{landslide} \mid SI, \text{rain}) \times E[\text{deaths} \mid \text{landslide}].
$$

Rainfall is the prediction year's, and the severity covariates do not vary by scenario, so the
severity expectation is computed once per tile and reused. The scenarios differ only through the
stability index that enters the hazard probability -- which is to say, only through root cohesion.

**Avoided mortality** is then the counterfactual minus the observed:

$$
\text{avoided deaths} \;=\; \text{deaths}_{\text{full\_impacts}} \;-\; \text{deaths}_{\text{observed}}.
$$

Physically this cannot be negative -- removing root cohesion cannot make a slope safer -- so pixels
where it comes out negative are counted and warned about rather than silently floored.

## Valuation

Avoided deaths are priced at the **value of a statistical life**, per country, in 2019 constant USD
to match the rest of GEP.

Countries with a published OECD country estimate take it directly. The published figures are 2022 USD
and are reported with a power-of-ten multiplier, so they are scaled up and then deflated to 2019
using the PMPRB CPI-based cumulative price-adjustment factor of 1.050 from 2019 to 2022.

Countries without a direct estimate take their income group's figure from Table 6.1 of OECD (2025),
*Mortality Risk Valuation in Policy Assessment*: 7.1 USD million for high-income OECD, 7.9 for
high-income non-OECD, and 1.1 for the upper-middle, lower-middle and low-income groups. A row whose
income group is unclassified takes the global figure of 2.7 USD million. These are 2022 USD millions
and are deflated the same way.

The per-country values are joined onto the EE r264 correspondence and rasterized onto the 1km grid,
so every pixel carries its country's VSL. The service's value raster is the avoided-death raster
times the VSL raster, and country totals are the zonal sums of both rasters over the correspondence
polygons.

Note that the r264 correspondence splits large countries into sub-regions. Each sub-region carries
its country's ISO3 and therefore its national VSL, which is what the rasterization needs; a
one-row-per-country table has to sum the sub-regions back together, which is what the results report
does.

## What the module does not do

- The stability model is static: one specific discharge from a climatological rainfall normal, not an
  event-based or seasonal hydrology.
- Rainfall enters the hazard model as the annual maximum daily total, so hazard is a per-pixel-year
  probability, not a per-storm one.
- Transmissivity units are flagged as unverified in the code and have not been checked against the
  HiHydroSoil documentation here.
- The module has been run end to end once on the cluster, but its numbers have not been replicated
  against a machine-readable v0.2.0 output from the author, so they remain provisional.

## References

The citations below are the ones the code itself names. They are the model family and the specific
corrections applied, not a general literature review.

1. Duan, N. (1983). Smearing estimate: a nonparametric retransformation method.
2. Horn, B. K. P. (1981). Hill shading and the reflectance map. (The slope algorithm `gdal.DEMProcessing` uses.)
3. OECD (2025). *Mortality Risk Valuation in Policy Assessment*, Table 6.1.
4. Prentice, R. L., and Pyke, R. (1979). Logistic disease incidence models and case-control studies.
